questions.prompt: A singly linked list contains keys 1,2,...,n in this order. Which operation can delete the node containing key n in O(1) time if only a pointer to that node is given?
options: Yes, by setting its next to null
Yes, by copying its predecessor's next value
questions.explanation: Without the predecessor pointer, the previous link cannot be changed; copying the successor's data fails for the tail. The head pointer also does not identify the predecessor.

questions.prompt: A pointer p addresses a non-tail node in a singly linked list. Which method deletes p in O(1) time when node payloads may be copied?
options: Copy successor payload into p and bypass successor
answer: Copy successor payload into p and bypass successor
questions.explanation: Copying the successor's payload into p and linking p to the successor's successor removes the logical element in constant time, provided p is not the tail and payload copying is allowed.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has n nodes. Starting only at head, how many next-pointer traversals are needed to reach the node at zero-based position k, where 0<=k<n?
questions.explanation: The head is at position zero, so exactly k links are followed to reach position k.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list has a tail pointer t and n>=1 nodes. Which pointer identifies its first node?
questions.explanation: In a circular list, the tail's next link points to the head; this provides head access in constant time.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list supports insertion at the front and deletion at the front. What is the worst-case time for each?
questions.explanation: Insertion changes the new node's next and the head pointer. Deletion advances head to head.next. Both take constant pointer operations.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is unsorted and has no tail pointer. Which operations have worst-case O(1) time?
options: Insert a node at the head
Append a node at the tail
Find whether a given key occurs

questions.prompt: A linked list has n nodes. A complete traversal follows the next pointer of every node except the last. How many next-pointer traversals occur?
questions.explanation: Each of the first n-1 nodes links to its successor; the last node has no successor link to follow.

questions.prompt: Two nonempty singly linked lists are concatenated in O(1) time when both head and tail pointers are maintained. Which update is required?
options: First tail.next becomes second head, then first tail becomes second tail
No update is possible in O(1)
answer: First tail.next becomes second head, then first tail becomes second tail
questions.explanation: The first tail is linked to the second head, and the resulting tail is the second list's tail. Both list endpoints are available directly.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is represented only by a head pointer. What is the worst-case time to append one node?
questions.explanation: The implementation must traverse to the last node to set its next field. Without a tail pointer this scan is linear.

questions.prompt: For a doubly linked list with head and tail pointers, which operations take O(1) time?
options: Insert before a node when its pointer is given
Delete a node when its pointer is given
Find the predecessor of a node when its pointer is given
Find a key by value in an unsorted list

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list node x is deleted from a nonempty list. Which pair of neighbor updates is generally required?
questions.explanation: For an interior node, reconnecting the predecessor to the successor and the successor to the predecessor removes x. Boundary cases update head or tail instead.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list contains 7 nodes. Starting at head, how many next-pointer traversals return to head for the first time?
questions.explanation: A cycle through all seven distinct nodes returns to its starting node after exactly seven link traversals.

questions.prompt: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm starts both pointers at the head of a list with a cycle of length lambda and a noncyclic prefix of length mu. What is its worst-case time order?
questions.explanation: The pointers advance one and two links per iteration. They meet within O(mu+lambda) steps, requiring linear time in the prefix plus cycle length.

questions.prompt: Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm uses two pointers advancing by one and two links. Which statement is correct for an acyclic list of n nodes?
options: It terminates after O(n) steps without a meeting
It always meets at the tail
answer: It terminates after O(n) steps without a meeting
questions.explanation: On an acyclic list the fast pointer eventually reaches null (or its next is null), so the algorithm terminates after linear traversal with constant extra space.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has a cycle consisting of 5 nodes. Once Floyd's slow and fast pointers are both within the cycle, what is the maximum number of iterations until they meet?
questions.explanation: Their relative speed is one node per iteration modulo the cycle length. Any initial separation is removed in at most lambda iterations, here five.

questions.prompt: A list is reversed iteratively using prev, cur, and next pointers. After processing the first k nodes of an n-node list, which invariant holds?
options: prev heads the reversed prefix and cur heads the untouched suffix
prev is always null and cur heads the reversed prefix
The original head still heads the whole list
The tail points to the original head
answer: prev heads the reversed prefix and cur heads the untouched suffix
questions.explanation: Each processed link is reversed toward prev, so prev is the head of the reversed prefix and cur begins the remaining original-order suffix.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list of 9 nodes is reversed iteratively. How many next pointers of existing nodes must be redirected?
questions.explanation: Every original edge between consecutive nodes is reversed; a list of nine nodes has eight such edges.

questions.prompt: To find the middle node of a singly linked list in one pass using slow and fast pointers, how should they advance?
options: Slow by one and fast by two links
Slow by two and fast by one link
Fast by three and slow by two links
answer: Slow by one and fast by two links
questions.explanation: The fast pointer traverses twice as quickly. When it reaches the end, slow has traversed approximately half the list.

questions.prompt: A list has 8 nodes. With slow initialized at head and fast at head, and the loop condition fast!=null && fast.next!=null followed by slow=slow.next and fast=fast.next.next, where does slow stop?
questions.explanation: For an even-length list under this initialization and loop, slow advances four times and stops at index 4, the second of the two central nodes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about singly linked-list traversal are true?
options: Accessing position k from head takes O(k) time
Finding the predecessor of a given node pointer may require O(n) time
A tail pointer alone makes arbitrary indexed access O(1)
Searching an unsorted list is O(n) in the worst case
answer: Accessing position k from head takes O(k) time
Finding the predecessor of a given node pointer may require O(n) time
Searching an unsorted list is O(n) in the worst case
questions.explanation: Links provide sequential access, so indexed access and predecessor search may scan linearly. A tail pointer only helps at the end, and unsorted key search is linear.
